newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First revamps its compulsory pension scheme.
newsitem.headline: NZ First revamps its compulsory pension scheme.

text.p: New Zealand First on Monday released a revamped version of its compulsory superannuation policy, including the scrapping of the government guarantee and the introduction of a government contribution for those who care for children and dependents.
The changes to NZ First's July policy, were released in a paper distributed to the news media on Sunday.

Nationalist NZ First, which holds the balance of power after the October 12 election, is negotiating separately with the conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party over the shape of the next government.
NZ First's superannuation policy has been a major sticking point in both sets of talks.
The parties have said they expect a coalition proposal to be put to their caucuses either this week or next week.
The eight-page NZ First superannuation paper does not explain the reason for the changes.

When party leader Winston Peters launched the original policy before the election he said there would be government guarantees on investment returns, but today's paper said: "The current intention is to have no more guarantees than the current voluntary schemes have," although it adds the government may offer protection against fraud.
It has dropped plans to exempt the first $5000 of income from the scheme.
It is now proposing contributors be allowed to borrow from the fund at low or zero interest rates to buy their own homes, obtain vocational training and set up businesses.
The self-employed would pay only a minimal amount recognising they are already investing heavily in their business, the paper said.

The NZ First scheme would see a levy of three percent of earnings and benefit income from those below the retirement age. That would rise by one percentage point a year until it reaches eight percent in 2002.
It would operate as a second tier superannuation scheme. On retirement the invested funds would be converted into an annuity.
The first tier, universal, New Zealand Superannuation would be retained at or near the current 35 percent of the average wage for each one of a married couple.
